Sanskrit & Yogic Psychology
TermDefinition
Atman The individual self, in Vedanta — but held as identical to, not separate from, universal consciousness. Not "a soul" in the sense of a separate possession; closer to the awareness doing the possessing.
Brahman The ground of all reality in Vedanta — not a deity to petition, but the substrate everything, including you, is made of and never actually separate from.
Jiva The individual, experiencing self — distinct from Atman only in that Jiva is Atman as it appears bound to one particular body and story. Same light, wearing a name.
Maya Usually translated "illusion," though "the measuring-out" is closer — the way one undivided reality appears to us as separate things, separate selves, and passing time.
Chitta The mind-stuff, or memory-store — the layer that holds impressions, conditioning, and habitual patterns built up over time. Not thought itself, but the substrate thought leaves marks on.
Antahkarana Literally "the inner instrument" — the collective term in Vedanta for mind, intellect, and ego-sense together: the machinery through which consciousness processes experience.
Ahamkara Literally "the I-maker" — the function of mind that takes raw experience and stamps "me" onto it, manufacturing a sense of separate identity out of what's actually happening.
Manas The lower mind, one of Antahkarana's four components — the part that registers sense data and flickers between options, before any real discernment happens.
Buddhi The discerning intellect, one of Antahkarana's four components — the part that actually judges and decides, one step up from Manas.
Annamaya (Kosha) The "food sheath" — the physical body itself, the most outer and dense of the traditional five layers (koshas) said to wrap the true Self. Not just a label: the Chandogya Upanishad traces this body to three elemental strands — fire, water, earth — interwoven in everything, including you, each refining through three grades. Solid food's coarsest residue is faeces, its middle grade is flesh, its finest is mind. Water's coarsest is urine, its middle is blood, its finest is breath. Fire's coarsest is bone, its middle is marrow, its finest is voice. Compressed to one line: the mind is made of food, the breath is made of water, the voice is made of heat.
Asanaya (Hunger) Water leading food along inside the body — the Upanishads' own etymology for hunger, built from a root meaning "to lead" or "to carry" (the same root behind gonaya, "a leader of cows"). Hunger, on this reading, is not an alarm bell but one element quietly moving another.
Udanya (Thirst) Fire evaporating water inside the body — the structural twin of Asanaya. What's left over once fire finishes with water gets a name of its own: heat, the residue neither element claimed.
Svapiti (Sleep) Sleep's own Sanskrit verb, traditionally glossed as sva apitah — "he enters himself." Not biological shutdown on this reading, but a forced nightly return: the waking mind, worn out from circling the external world in search of somewhere final to rest, finds nothing out there and is driven back into its own root.
Prana Vital, life-giving energy carried on the breath — not the breath itself (the physical inhale/exhale), and not Pranamaya, the subtler “sheath” it is said to constitute. In this framework, Prana is what gives the raw intake of air its rhythmic meaning at Layer 2: Breath.
Pranamaya (Kosha) The "breath/vital-energy sheath" — one layer in from the physical body: the layer of life-force, circulation, and breath that animates it.
Puraka Inhalation — drawing breath in, traditionally done through the nose, evenly and without strain.
Kumbhaka Retention — suspending the breath, on either side of the inhale or exhale.
Rechaka Exhalation — releasing breath out, traditionally paced slower than or equal to the inhale.
Nadi A channel the traditional physiology maps subtle energy moving through — not a nerve in the anatomical sense, though the two get compared.
Ida The left-side channel in Hatha Yoga physiology, associated with the cooling, lunar current.
Pingala The right-side channel in Hatha Yoga physiology, associated with the heating, solar current.
Sushumna The central channel in Hatha Yoga physiology, said to run along the spine — the one Ida and Pingala are meant to balance into.
Manomaya (Kosha) The "mind sheath" — the layer of thought, emotion, and sensory processing; where most people spend nearly all their time without noticing it's a layer at all.
Vijnanamaya (Kosha) The "wisdom/intellect sheath" — the layer of discernment and insight, one step subtler than ordinary thought: the part that can actually notice the mind sheath working.
Anandamaya (Kosha) The "bliss sheath" — the innermost and subtlest of the five, closer to the Self than to the intellect. Not a mood you generate, but what's left when nothing else is being generated. Doesn't correspond to its own row in the 7-layer matrix above — it sits just inside Layer 4 (Vijnanamaya), wrapping directly around Layer 7 (Atman).
Yogic & Sanskrit Concepts
TermDefinition
Vritti A fluctuation or wave of the mind-stuff (Chitta) — the constant stream of mental chatter, images, and fleeting concepts stirred up by the senses, rippling across an otherwise still lake of awareness.
Nirodha Stilling, or restraint — the word Patanjali uses in Yoga Sutra 1.2 to define yoga itself: the stilling of the mind's fluctuations (Vritti).
Bhava The felt, energetic weight a thought or state carries — nostalgia clinging to a memory, anxiety clinging to the future. Not the thought itself, but the charge riding on it.
Purusha Pure consciousness, in Samkhya and Yoga philosophy — unmoving, unchanging, the witness that never itself becomes an object. Not a mixture with Prakriti, but what watches Prakriti happen.
Prakriti Nature itself, in Samkhya and Yoga philosophy — everything that changes, moves, and evolves: matter, mind, thought, and emotion, as distinct from the still consciousness (Purusha) observing it.
Abhyasa Sustained, uninterrupted practice, applied over a long stretch of time — the effort side of steadying the mind, paired with Vairagya as its counterpart.
Vairagya Dispassion, or non-attachment — not the absence of desire, but the absence of thirst for what desire promises. A finished taste, not a suppressed one.
Avidya Literally "not-seeing" — the root ignorance that mistakes the temporary, changing self for the true, unchanging one. The starting condition every path of self-inquiry works to dissolve.
Gunas The three fundamental qualities that make up all of Prakriti (nature) — Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. Every object, thought, mood, and meal is some shifting mixture of the three; not moral categories, but the raw material personality and matter are both built from.
Moha Delusion — the basic clouding of judgment that mistakes the false for the real. The functional end-state of unchecked conditioning left to run in the dark.
Vipallasa A perceptual distortion, in Buddhist psychology — seeing the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, the painful as pleasurable, the not-self as self.
Sattva One of the three Gunas — the quality of lightness, clarity, and spiritual luminosity in Prakriti. The mind is calm enough here to see what's actually there, undistorted by craving (Rajas) or dulled by inertia (Tamas) — the condition under which self-knowledge becomes possible.
Rajas One of the three Gunas — the quality of energy, passion, and ceaseless movement. In balance: motivation, creativity, sustained effort. Out of balance: restlessness, anxiety, and desire-driven action. The indispensable bridge between Tamas and Sattva — without Rajas, nothing moves.
Tamas One of the three Gunas — the quality of heaviness, inertia, and darkness. In balance: necessary rest, grounding, timely sleep. Out of balance: dullness, confusion, and resistance to change. The heaviest of the three — and the starting point every ascent toward Sattva begins from.
Samskara A subconscious impression left behind by a past thought, emotion, or action, which conditions future thought and behavior — the mechanism behind habit, and behind Karma.
Nirvana The Buddhist term for the extinguishing of the fires of craving, aversion, and delusion — release from the cycle of suffering, often used interchangeably with Moksha across traditions.
Dharma One's right action or duty in a given moment — not a fixed rulebook handed down from outside, but what is actually called for by your nature, circumstance, and stage on the path.
Kama Desire — wish, longing, or sensory pleasure; one of the four traditional aims of life (Purusharthas) alongside duty, prosperity, and liberation. In this framework, the raw craving that hardens into a constructed identity (Ahamkara).
Karma The law of cause and effect applied to action and intention — every deed, thought, and reaction leaves an imprint (Samskara) that shapes what comes next.
Samsara The wheel of birth, death, and rebirth — the ceaseless, cyclical churn of conditioned existence every layer below the Self remains bound to. Not chaos in the sense of meaningless disorder, but the spinning, tension-filled dance every unliberated thing is caught inside, until Moksha or Nirvana breaks the cycle.
Moksha Liberation — release from the cycle of rebirth and from mistaken identity with the small self. The Vedantic term for the same recognition Buddhism calls Nirvana.
Yama The outward restraints — non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing — first limb of Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga, governing how you act toward others.
Niyama The inward observances — contentment, purity, discipline — second limb of Ashtanga Yoga, governing how you treat yourself.
Asana Posture, third limb of Ashtanga Yoga — traditionally just a seat stable enough to let the body be forgotten.
Pranayama Control of the breath, fourth limb of Ashtanga Yoga — not breathing exercises for their own sake, but the deliberate use of breath to steady the mind that rides on it.
Pratyahara Withdrawal of the senses from their objects, fifth limb of Ashtanga Yoga — the hinge between the outer four limbs and the inner three, where attention stops chasing the senses and turns inward.
Ekagrata One-pointedness — the literal quality Dharana, the sixth limb, trains the mind toward.
Dharana Single-pointed concentration — the sixth limb of Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga. Binding the mind-stuff (Chitta) onto one object, on purpose, against its habit of scattering. Effortful by nature — the deliberate work that makes Dhyana possible.
Dhyana Sustained, uninterrupted meditative flow — the seventh limb, and the natural evolution of Dharana. The effort of "trying to focus" dissolves; what remains is an unbroken stream of attention toward the object. The bridge between concentration and Samadhi.
Samadhi The state in which the external form of an object of meditation is given up entirely and only its essential meaning remains — absorption without separation between observer and observed.
The Seven Chakras
TermDefinition
Chakra Sanskrit for “wheel” — one of the body’s psychic energy centers in the yogic and tantric traditions, traditionally mapped along the spine from base to crown. This framework borrows the seven-chakra ladder as a map for how consciousness itself matures, using each chakra as a different operating altitude of awareness rather than a location to unblock.
Root Chakra (Muladhara) The base of the ladder — operating on the consciousness of physical survival, material form, and biology. In this framework it governs Layer 1: Body, from the first claiming of physical space in the womb to the body’s return to the earth at death.
Sacral Chakra (Svadhisthana) Operating on the consciousness of life-force, emotional baseline, and vital rhythm. In this framework it governs Layer 2: Breath, from the first cry that floods the lungs with air to the last exhalation that dissolves individual life-force back into the atmosphere.
Solar Plexus Chakra (Manipura) Operating on the consciousness of linear logic, everyday perception, and sensory processing. In this framework it governs Layer 3: Mind, from a newborn’s first overwhelming sensory input to the fading of the senses at the end of life.
Heart Chakra (Anahata) Operating on the consciousness of structural truth, objective logic, and core beliefs. In this framework it governs Layer 4: Intellect, from a child’s first curiosity about existence to an elder’s lifetime of wisdom offered forward as a kind of art.
Throat Chakra (Vishuddha) Operating on the consciousness of systemic patterns, karma, and personal history. In this framework it governs Layer 5: Memory, from a person’s first impression to the eventual erasure of ego-memory into the collective unconscious.
Third Eye Chakra (Ajna) Operating on the consciousness of individual identity, self-will, and personal archetype. In this framework it governs Layer 6: Ego, from a toddler’s first sense that “I am separate” to the eventual dissolution of that separate self.
Crown Chakra (Sahasrara) The summit of the ladder — operating on the highest consciousness of the Eternal Witness, unity, and absolute transcendence. In this framework it governs Layer 7: Self / Soul, the one layer said to stand entirely outside time, birth, and death.
The Four States (AUM)
TermDefinition
AUM The primal sound-symbol of Vedanta, mapped here to the four states of consciousness: A is Jagrat (waking), U is Svapna (dreaming), M is Prajna (deep sleep) — and the silence after the sound stops is Turiya, the awareness underneath all three.
Jagrat The ordinary waking state — consciousness engaged with the external, physical world through the senses.
Svapna The dream state — consciousness turned inward, generating its own world out of memory and imagination while the body rests.
Prajna Deep, dreamless sleep — no object of any kind, waking or dream, yet not nothing: you wake up and know you slept well, which means something was present to know it.
Turiya The "fourth" state — not another state alongside waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, but the constant awareness present underneath all three, witnessing each without changing when they change.
Vishva Waking consciousness bound to a single body — the individual counterpart to Virat, the same state at cosmic, unbound scale.
Taijasa Dream consciousness bound to a single sleeping body — the individual counterpart to Hiranyagarbha, the same state at cosmic scale.
Ishvara Deep sleep at cosmic scale — the individual counterpart is Prajna. Not ignorance of the world, but the causal stillness everything else rests on.
Virat The physical cosmic manifestation — the universe itself, considered as a single body. The cosmic counterpart to Vishva.
Hiranyagarbha Literally the "golden womb" — the universal "I-Am," pure self-consciousness arising before any physical form exists. The cosmic counterpart to Taijasa.
Alchemical Stages
TermDefinition
Lead (Base Matter) The heaviest, most inert starting material in alchemy — the raw, unrefined condition everything else in the sequence works on.
Copper (Purification) An early refining stage — impurities in the base material start burning off, but the result is still volatile and unstable.
Iron (Strength) A hardening stage — the volatility of the previous stage sets into something rigid and load-bearing, for better and worse.
Silver (Refinement) A polishing stage — the rigid material of the last stage gets refined into something more responsive and reflective, without yet reaching gold's stability.
Gold (Illumination) The classical alchemical goal-material — incorruptible, stable, "illuminated." What the earlier, cruder stages were always in service of becoming.
Quintessence Literally the "fifth essence" — beyond the four classical elements (earth, water, air, fire), the pure spirit or vital essence said to underlie and animate all of them.
Philosopher’s Stone The legendary end-goal of alchemy — not a literal object but a completed transformation, capable of "turning lead into gold": in this framework, base conditioning fully transmuted into realized SELF.
The Seven Hermetic Principles
TermDefinition
Mentalism "The All is Mind." The principle that the universe is fundamentally mental in nature — matter as a mode of mind, not the other way around.
Correspondence "As above, so below." The principle that the same patterns repeat at every scale — a single moment of reaction contains the same structure as a lifetime's conditioning.
Vibration "Nothing rests; everything moves." The principle that all matter, energy, thought, and spirit are in constant motion — stillness is always relative, never absolute.
Polarity "Everything is dual; opposites are identical in nature, differing only in degree." Hot and cold are the same phenomenon, temperature, at different points — not two separate things.
Rhythm "Everything flows, out and in; everything has its tides." The principle that all things swing between poles in a measurable rhythm — including moods, motivation, and insight.
Cause & Effect "Every cause has its effect; every effect has its cause." Nothing happens by pure chance — what looks random is usually a cause operating on a plane you haven't traced yet.
Gender "Gender is in everything." Not biological sex — a generative/receptive polarity present in all creation, thought, and action, the interplay that produces anything new.
Theosophy & Subtle Bodies
TermDefinition
Thought-Form In the clairvoyant taxonomy of Annie Besant and C.W. Leadbeater (1901), the second, detachable effect of every thought — a floating form built of astral matter, coloured by the thought's quality and shaped by its nature, that travels until it discharges its energy on a mind vibrating in sympathy with it. See The Pain-Body for a modern description of the same basic mechanism.
Kama-Manas The lower, desire-driven mind — Manas (thought) fused with Kama (desire/passion) — identified in this tradition as the animating charge inside a thought-form. Compare Manas above.
Astral Plane / Astral Body The subtler layer of substance, in this and related traditions, said to sit just beyond ordinary matter — the medium a thought-form is built from and travels through, and the vehicle through which emotion is felt.
(Artificial) Elemental This tradition's term for a thought-form once it is complete — a temporary, semi-autonomous entity with an outer shell of quickened elemental essence wrapped around the thinker's own mental energy as its core.
Brainwave & Awareness States
TermDefinition
Delta (0.5–4 Hz) The slowest brainwave band, dominant in deep, dreamless sleep — the conscious mind is fully offline while the body repairs itself.
Theta (4–8 Hz) Active during the twilight zone between waking and sleep, or deep meditation — attention turns inward toward imagery, intuition, and dreams.
Alpha (8–12 Hz) The state of calm, relaxed wakefulness — an "idling" visual system, often peaking when the eyes close and the mind drifts.
Mu (8–13 Hz) Shares Alpha's frequency but sits over the motor cortex — the body idling in neutral, present during physical stillness and vanishing the instant you move, or even intend to.
Beta (12–30 Hz) The everyday waking state — dominant when attention is directed outward: solving problems, conversing, making decisions.
Gamma (30–100 Hz) The fastest standard brainwave band, associated with binding information across brain regions into one coherent experience — present during peak focus and sudden insight. See the research note →
Lambda (100+ Hz) A rarely-observed, very high frequency band associated with profound meditative or altered states — deep stillness paired with rapid, high-coherence processing.
Clinical & Scientific
TermDefinition
Senescence The point where cells stop dividing and repairing themselves as efficiently — the biological beginning of decline, before outright breakdown. On the Master Matrix, this is the stage between Aging and Mortality at every layer above the body too, from the Mind's Fatigue to the Ego's Rigidity.
Information Integration A measure of how much different regions of the brain are combining what they're processing into one unified picture, rather than just being separately active. See the research note →
